original_question: Given a countable homogeneous structure K, and for each finite substructure A of K letting the big Ramsey degree T(A) mean the least positive integer T such that every finite coloring of the copies of A in K has a subcopy of K in which at most T colors remain, does every finite A have such a degree, and if so can the exact degrees be characterized by canonical partitions and computed algorithmically?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Question 2.3(1)-(2), read together with Question 1.3 for the definition of big Ramsey degree and Definition 2.4 for the meaning of canonical partition.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the paper’s two-part guiding question about big Ramsey degrees for a homogeneous structure K: first, whether every finite substructure A has a big Ramsey degree T(A), and second, whether, assuming those degrees exist, the exact values can be characterized via canonical partitions and then computed or algorithmically determined. Your definition of T(A) is substantively faithful to the paper’s definition.
missing_details: The paper works in the setting of a finite relational language L; the question is not posed for arbitrary structures with function symbols or in a non-relational setting.
In this paper, unless otherwise specified, 'homogeneous' means countably infinite homogeneous.
The finite structures A under discussion are the members of Age(K), i.e. the finite structures that embed into K.
The paper explicitly treats copies of A in K as images of embeddings and uses the standard notation for the set of copies of A in K.
Question 2.3(1) is phrased not only as existence of T(A), but as asking whether one can find upper bounds ensuring that big Ramsey degrees exist for all finite A.
Question 2.3(2) is conditional: it asks for a characterization of exact big Ramsey degrees via canonical partitions only after assuming that K has finite big Ramsey degrees.

To make 'via canonical partitions' stand alone, one must define a canonical partition: for every finite coloring of the copies of A in K, there is a subcopy K' isomorphic to K such that each partition piece becomes monochromatic on K', and each piece persists by meeting every subcopy K' of K.

The paper distinguishes 'finite big Ramsey degrees' from 'exact big Ramsey degrees are known': the latter means either the degrees are explicitly computed or there is a characterization from which they can be computed.

The paper treats the stronger nearby question of whether K carries a big Ramsey structure as a separate part of the program; your draft should not fold that stronger notion into the canonical-partition question unless stated explicitly.
refined_question: Let K be a countably infinite homogeneous relational structure in a finite relational language, and let Age(K) be its age. For each finite A in Age(K), let T(A) denote the least positive integer such that every finite coloring of the set of copies of A in K has a subcopy K' isomorphic to K in which at most T(A) colors appear on the copies of A. Does K have finite big Ramsey degrees, in the sense that such a T(A) exists for every finite A (equivalently, can one find upper bounds guaranteeing existence of these degrees)? If K does have finite big Ramsey degrees, is there a characterization of the exact values T(A) via canonical partitions of the copies of A in K—where a canonical partition means one whose pieces are forced to be monochromatic on some subcopy K' isomorphic to K under every finite coloring and each piece persists in every such subcopy—and, if so, can the exact degrees be calculated or algorithmically determined from that characterization?
justification: The draft is aiming at the paper’s general two-step guiding problem about big Ramsey degrees, not at a later special-case open problem. Question 1.3 supplies the definition of T(A). Question 2.3(1) then asks exactly whether a given homogeneous structure K has finite big Ramsey degrees, and Question 2.3(2) asks whether, assuming finiteness, the exact degrees can be characterized via canonical partitions and calculated or algorithmically found. Definition 2.4 gives the formal content of 'canonical partition'. The nearby stronger question about big Ramsey structures is treated separately in Question 2.3(3) and later as Problem 6.3, so it should not be merged into the refined question unless explicitly intended.
